{"id": "26:21/q13", "question": "What is the ḥukm God gave Moses?", "turns_on": "Whether ḥukm names prophethood itself, a distinct cognitive or practical gift, the Torah's law, divine grace, or transcendent wisdom; the following mention of messengership and the Torah's later date are explicit tests.", "positions": [{"id": "26:21/q13/p1", "position": "Prophethood, sometimes understood together with its wisdom and knowledge.", "reasons": "Al-Suddi is cited by Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim, Wahidi, Qurtubi, Durr and Alusi; Ibn Abbas by Wahidi. Ibn Atiyya includes prophetic wisdom; Nasafi and Kuran Yolu include knowledge too. Abu Hayyan and Bursevi's Fath al-Rahman say messengerhood then adds a higher rank. Ibn Ashur places the beginning when God spoke to Moses."}, {"id": "26:21/q13/p2", "position": "Knowledge, understanding, sound judgment, intellect or divinely given guidance.", "reasons": "Maqatil is cited for knowledge and understanding by Wahidi, Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi; Jishumi prefers this because messengerhood is paired separately. Razi similarly prefers knowledge over prophethood because the next clause names the latter; he includes reason, judgment and knowledge of divine unity as needed for a messenger. Tabrisi includes knowing wisdom's demands, Torah, lawful and unlawful matters, and rulings. Biqai specifies practical knowledge fit for wise judges. Tabataba'i specifies insight into reality applied skillfully to action; he compares stages of soundness in childhood and mature reasoning and cites 3:79, 6:89 and 45:16 for distinguishing judgment from prophethood. Islahi connects it to divine guidance needed beyond uprightness and intellect, citing 11:17 and 26:83. Study Quran also mentions decision-making power, intelligence and understanding; Alusi says some restrict the knowledge to what distinguishes prophethood."}, {"id": "26:21/q13/p3", "position": "The Torah or its divine legal judgments.", "reasons": "Zajjaj identifies the Torah because it contains God's legal judgments; Qurtubi cites him. Tabrisi includes the Torah among the contents of knowledge, while Tabataba'i sees it as a later culmination of growing judgment after Pharaoh drowned, citing 5:43. Wahidi objects that the Torah was given only after Pharaoh drowned."}, {"id": "26:21/q13/p4", "position": "Divine graces (luṭf).", "reasons": "Razi reports the Muʿtazilite explanation but calls it very weak because grace is given to all without withholding, so its specification here requires a reason."}, {"id": "26:21/q13/p5", "position": "Wisdom beyond demonstration, acquisition and reason.", "reasons": "Qashani gives this inward account and says God made Moses a messenger with that wisdom."}]}

{"id": "26:21/q15", "question": "What does being made one of the messengers add to the gift of ḥukm?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase merely identifies Moses' prophetic company, marks a rank beyond prophethood, or stresses the source and standing of his commission.", "positions": [{"id": "26:21/q15/p1", "position": "It says Moses was included among the prophets and sent as God's messenger.", "reasons": "Jishumi and Tabrisi gloss the group as the prophets. {"id": "26:21/q16", "question": "How does Moses' account of flight and divine appointment answer Pharaoh?", "turns_on": "Whether the emphasis falls on Moses' newly granted authority or on Pharaoh's culpability and claimed favor.", "positions": [{"id": "26:21/q16/p1", "position": "His present God-given wisdom and mission supersede the earlier killing and establish his authority now.", "reasons": "Baydawi says wisdom and messengership answer Pharaoh's attempt to discredit prophecy through the killing. Razi contrasts God's benefit with Pharaoh's wrongdoing. Ibn Kathir says obedience now brings safety and defiance ruin. Ibn Ashur calls the sequence purposeful because present state and final outcome matter more than the past. Islahi says Pharaoh must hear Moses without dwelling on the past. Tabataba'i says prior familiarity predicts only acquired status, whereas this mission is divine. Samarrai links the reply to 26:18–19."}, {"id": "26:21/q16/p2", "position": "The flight exposes Pharaoh's treatment of Moses as harmful rather than a favor.", "reasons": "Razi says Pharaoh's threat caused Moses' fear and flight, leaving Pharaoh no favor regarding the killing. Baydawi says Moses does not deny the true upbringing but treats it as a calamity stemming from Israelite enslavement; Samarrai says he overturns Pharaoh's boast by naming that enslavement."}]}
{"id": "26:21/q17", "question": "How do the notes assess Moses' earlier killing?", "turns_on": "Whether the note concerns intent, moral recognition, or frank acknowledgment of the past act.", "positions": [{"id": "26:21/q17/p1", "position": "It was unintended: his blow was meant as discipline.", "reasons": "Alusi gives the intended purpose of the blow. {"id": "26:21/q18", "question": "What guidance is drawn from Moses' fear and flight?", "turns_on": "Whether the flight illustrates prudent protection, the spiritual consequences of fearing God, or a divinely induced retreat.", "positions": [{"id": "26:21/q18/p1", "position": "One may flee danger when unable to resist, and a believer should seek a place where religion is safe.", "reasons": "Sulami reports that flight from what cannot be endured is the conduct of messengers; Abu Bakr al-Warraq specifies protection from desire, innovation and misguidance. {"id": "26:21/q19", "question": "What inward condition does the surrounding exchange depict?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:21/q19/p1", "position": "The veiled self cannot know the Real, prophetic wisdom or religious law and resists revelation.", "reasons": "Qashani describes it as asserting itself, resisting obedience and seeking to overpower revelation."}]}

Al-Wahidi likens this to claiming credit after killing someone's parents. Ibn Ashur mentions Pharaoh's wife finding him (28:9). Al-Biqa'i adds Joseph's earlier benefit to Egypt. Tabataba'i reports this view, without endorsing it. Al-Wahidi prefers denial overall."}, {"id": "26:22/q01/p2", "position": "Moses acknowledges being raised and spared as a personal favor, while contrasting Pharaoh's e

{"id": "26:22/q02", "question": "What does تمنها mean and what does reminding someone of a favor imply?", "turns_on": "Whether mann denotes the act of giving or the speech that recounts it.", "positions": [{"id": "26:22/q02/p1", "position": "It means to count, mention, or boast of a favor to someone.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi derives it from enumerating a favor and says the present tense evokes Pharaoh's scene. {"id": "26:22/q05", "question": "Is the opening of Moses's reply an unstated question or a declarative rebuke?", "turns_on": "Whether Arabic permits omitting a meaning-bearing interrogative particle here, and whether rebuke requires a question.", "positions": [{"id": "26:22/q05/p1", "position": "It is an incredulous question with an omitted interrogative hamza or understood aw.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash and al-Nazm support omission with Arabic and poetic examples; Baghawi cites 21:34 and poems, including Umar ibn Abi Rabi'a. Al-Farra permits omission in doubt expressions such as ترى زيدا منطلقا; Ali ibn Sulayman calls this colloquial. Al-Qurtubi finds a poem proving omission without am, against al-Nahhas. Burhan and Itqan compare 6:76 and Ibn Muhaysin's 2:6 reading; al-Samin also connects 4:79. Al-Biqa'i says an unmarked question is concise and courteous."}, {"id": "26:22/q05/p2", "position": "The words are a statement whose wording itself rebukes Pharaoh; no hamza need be posited.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj reads a declarative rebuke. Al-Alusi and Tabataba'i dispute the implied wording."}]}

Al-Mubarrad makes an the subject, 'favor you claim' its predicate, and enslaving the explanation."}, {"id": "26:22/q06/p2", "position": "It is accusative or genitive after an omitted preposition, giving the cause: because Pharaoh enslaved Israel.", "reasons": "Al-Farra and al-Tabari allow accusative with the favor Pharaoh claims; al-Zajjaj explains the causative irony: persecution placed Moses in Pharaoh's care. Al-Samin separately allows genitive under bi. Al-Hawfi and al-Samin call it a purpose accusative."}, {"id": "26:22/q06/p3", "position": "It is the predicate of an omitted subject, 'it is your enslaving of Israel.'", "reasons": "Al-Samin and Bursevi supply the implicit subject; al-Alusi lists this among grammatical possibilities. {"id": "26:22/q16", "question": "Why is the n of نعمةٌ not assimilated into the following t?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:22/q16/p1", "position": "Tanwin at a word's end blocks the large assimilation here.", "reasons": "Al-Nashr lists tanwin among three agreed blockers, with a pronominal first ta and a first letter already doubled. {"id": "26:105/q01", "question": "What does the perfect verb كَذَّبَتْ convey about the duration of the denial?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:105/q01/p1", "position": "The denial continued from the beginning of Noah's preaching to its end.", "reasons": "Bursevī reads the perfect form as expressing sustained denial throughout Noah's mission."}]}
{"id": "26:105/q02", "question": "Why does كَذَّبَتْ have feminine agreement with قَوْمُ?", "turns_on": "Whether qawm itself licenses feminine agreement, an understood feminine collective supplies it, or the choice carries a rhetorical effect.", "positions": [{"id": "26:105/q02/p1", "position": "Qawm itself permits feminine agreement.", "reasons": "Majāz cites both masculine and feminine usage; Kashshāf, Rāzī, Bayḍāwī and Samīn cite the feminine diminutive quwayma. Nasafī and Ālūsī say the collective admits both genders; Abū Ḥayyān notes masculine pronouns later refer to its rational male members, and Samīn explains that by predominance. Bursevī also cites the feminine diminutive. Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports this as one analysis."}, {"id": "26:105/q02/p2", "position": "The verb agrees with an understood feminine sense, such as Noah's community, group or nation, while qawm is masculine.", "reasons": "Zajjāj, Abū Isḥāq as transmitted by Wāḥidī, Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī's report from Zajjāj, Abū Ḥayyān's alternative, and Ṭabāṭabāʾī's reported analysis explicitly retain masculine qawm. Thaʿlabī compares the Qur'anic expression 'the Bedouins said.' Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Qurṭubī invoke community or congregation; Samīn offers umma as an alternative, and Ālūsī offers umma or jamāʿa.
